items.full: More than 50 educational institutions have joined WordPress Credits , giving students worldwide a way to earn academic recognition for contributing to WordPress. The program had two participating institutions in September 2025 and four the following month. By June 2026, that number had reached 27, before passing 50 this October. The program launched with the University of Pisa and was announced at WordCamp Europe 2025. Since then, it has expanded through partnerships that connect students with experienced contributors and practical projects. The WordPress Credits dashboard recorded participating institutions across 17 countries as of October 19, including Bangladesh, Costa Rica, Spain, Bolivia, and Indonesia. Each institution can adapt the program to its academic requirements, allowing students to contribute as part of their studies. Students work with mentors on projects that reflect their interests and areas of study. They might translate WordPress, improve documentation, create learning materials, or contribute to development and testing. Alongside that work, they practice collaborating with others and responding to feedback, then present their contributions at the end of the program. By October 19, the dashboard recorded 364 graduates and student contributions across 18 WordPress teams. That work supports the software and resources people use throughout the WordPress community. Local contributors have helped establish these partnerships by introducing WordPress Credits to nearby schools and adapting it to local languages and educational settings. Mentors guide students through their first contributions, while sponsors provide support and resources. Educators help make that participation part of students’ academic work. Thank you to the students, educators, mentors, and supporters whose involvement has brought the program to more than 50 institutions. Institutions can include WordPress Credits in an existing course, offer it as an internship, or incorporate it into a final project. The program is available at no cost to partner institutions, with flexible formats to suit their students and curriculum. To get started, read how to launch a WordPress Credits program and register your institution’s interest through the program page .

items.title: CSS-Tricks, Version 20
items.desc: Things look a little different around here? I hope so because we just pushed a site redesign! Here's everything new with the 20th(!!) version of CSS-Tricks. CSS-Tricks, Version 20 originally handwritten and published with love on CSS-Tricks . You should really get the newsletter as well.
items.full: NVIDIA L4 GPUs. 5-second cold starts. Scale to zero when idle. I’ve been bashing on updating this site’s design for the last couple of weeks. It’s high time things get a fresh coat of paint, right? The last version of CSS-Tricks was pushed five years ago . That’s ancient in web (and dog) years. It’s not like the site has simply sat all that time. We pushed lots of changes and shipped new features, particularly since 2024 , but we never really got the paint brushes out of storage. Now, before there’s a chorus of “things don’t look thaaaat different” I want to say I’m rarely a fan of complete re-builds and tend to lean into iterative releases. And the new v20 theme is what I’d call an iterative rollup that’s worthy of a version bump. Let’s go over the most notable updates to see why. Excavating Ghosts First and foremost, some of the biggest changes are what you don’t see. As you might imagine, this site has carried over plenty of pieces across 19 years. I decided to excavate the theme and definitely found some ghosts to bust. For example, the global compiled JavaScript file retained some scripts that just weren’t being used anymore. Things like handling embedded versions of the newsletter from before we began self-hosting the posts. There were relics that catered specifically to the Flexbox Guide for handling toggles back before we had proper HTML <details> . There was a jQuery lazy-loader thing that is well-covered by WordPress core now. We had some scripts for serving third-party ads that are no longer needed now that we’re self-hosting ads. Things like that. The overall JavaScript was nicely trimmed from 151.6 KB (55.3 KB gzipped) to 133.8 KB (48.1 KB). I also decided to formally retire the CSS-Tricks Forum. We put it in “archive mode” back in, like, 2018. None of those discussions are particularly valuable for today as they were over 10 years ago, so I deactivated the bbPress plugin that powered it and cleared out the database… and wow, that carved a whopping 400 MB from the ol’ database, not to mention it allowed me to drop several custom templates from the theme. There were more ghosts busted along the way and, to be sure, there are still some lurking around. But it’s way less scary poking around the theme directory now, and further cleanup should be a lot easier from here on out. Modern Dev Tooling Yeah, yeah, raise your hand if you’re still running Gulp. We are 🙋‍♂️. That’s not a bad thing in and of itself, but keeping it in a fixed state for all this time is not the greatest. I think we’re sporting a more modern workflow than before, even if there’s still room to grow. A smattering of the related commits: For years, I endured the same errors every time I fired up a new terminal. Those are gone and things run super cleanly, not to mention quickly. Very happy here. Aside from being able to spot and fix a few unescaped custom field calls here and there, I decided to ask Claude to help me with a holistic audit. items.title: Tencent's AI chief says AI bioweapons are coming, but closing off models isn't the answer
items.desc: Tencent chief AI scientist Vinces Yao Shunyu warns that AI will soon be able to develop bioweapons and argues for a middle ground between open and closed models. While safety filters on open-source systems can be easily stripped through abliteration, closed models like Anthropic's Claude often block too aggressively. For its upcoming open-weight model Hy4, Tencent is filtering dangerous hacking knowledge directly from the training data. The article Tencent's AI chief says AI bioweapons are coming, but closing off models isn't the answer appeared first on The Decoder .
items.full: Tencent's AI chief says AI bioweapons are coming, but closing off models isn't the answer Maximilian Schreiner View the LinkedIn Profile of Maximilian Schreiner Nov 9, 2026 GPT-Image-2 prompted by THE DECODER Tencent's chief AI scientist warns that AI will soon be capable of developing bioweapons, and neither fully open nor fully closed models can solve this problem on their own. In the debate over open versus closed AI models, Vinces Yao Shunyu , formerly at OpenAI, is arguing for a middle ground, according to the South China Morning Post . A mix of open-source and closed-source lets everyone use the technology for defense as well. In biology, though, offensive and defensive capabilities are harder to separate than in cybersecurity. Since the gap between Chinese and US models isn't large, Yao urges the entire industry to proceed carefully. Yao says Anthropic and other US companies have made strong arguments for closed models, but he also sees clear advantages in open ones. He points to a hacking incident at Hugging Face as an example: when closed US models like Anthropic's Claude refused to analyze attack commands because of their safety filters, the platform used the open Chinese model GLM-5.2 to parse the logs instead. The Hugging Face report backs up Yao's example but also shows its limits. GLM-5.2 was only used during the forensic analysis. The actual attack was stopped when the security team patched the exploited vulnerability, rebuilt affected servers, and rotated credentials. Hugging Face also stressed that the incident isn't an argument against safety filters on hosted models. In July, Anthropic was the only major AI lab that didn't sign an Nvidia-backed letter warning against premature restrictions on open models. CEO Dario Amodei pushes back specifically against the claim that open models benefit defenders more than attackers. He argues they're potentially riskier because safety mechanisms are hard to enforce and published model weights can't be taken back. Anthropic doesn't call for an outright ban on open models, though. A technique called Abliteration shows how fragile safety filters are on open models. Anyone with access to a model's weights can use it to surgically remove trained refusal behaviors. Thousands of these modified variants sit on Hugging Face, and the US startup Abliteration.ai sells access to an unfiltered version of GLM-5.3. Current research shows that existing countermeasures make these modifications harder but don't prevent them. A more robust approach is to keep dangerous knowledge out of the model during training in the first place. China recognizes the problem too. The standards body TC260 warns that safety mechanisms in open models can be removed or bypassed and is working on its own security standard for open-source AI. A draft export control framework covers particularly large models but exempts open models that have already been released. Neither China nor the US has set a binding threshold above which open models can't be published. items.title: Google ships four TPU variants in one year as it ramps up competition with Nvidia
items.desc: Google is expanding its TPU 8 family with two specialized variants: the TPU 8tx keeps sensitive data encrypted even during processing, while the TPU 8i Max doubles compute power and memory by placing two chips on a single package. With nearly 100 external customers now on board, Google is increasingly positioning its in-house chips as an alternative to Nvidia's GPUs. The article Google ships four TPU variants in one year as it ramps up competition with Nvidia appeared first on The Decoder .
items.full: With two new TPU variants, Google is targeting confidential AI workloads and memory-hungry applications. The expansion cements Google's strategic shift toward positioning its in-house AI chips as a broad platform for external customers. Google has added two new systems to its eighth-generation AI accelerator lineup: the TPU 8tx for confidential computing and the TPU 8i Max for memory-intensive workloads. With these additions, Google says it has shipped four TPU systems within a single year for the first time. Both new variants are built on existing silicon. Google isn't introducing a new chip generation here, but new system configurations: different packaging, different networking, and different memory setups around the same processor. The company frames this modular approach as a deliberate design choice that lets it deliver new hardware variants in months rather than years. Ad The TPU 8tx targets enterprises and government agencies working with confidential data. Normally, data is encrypted during storage and transmission but has to be decrypted in memory once a processor works with it. Ad The TPU 8tx is designed to close that gap. According to Google, data and model weights stay protected and isolated even during active use. Nvidia already offers a comparable feature for GPUs through its confidential computing architecture. The system uses the same low-latency Boardfly network Google developed for real-time inference and is supposed to deliver up to twice the latency reduction compared to the TPU 8t. Google says enterprises can use a single system to fine-tune models, distill large models into smaller ones, and train AI agents with reinforcement learning, all without moving sensitive data between different clusters. Ad The TPU 8i Max tackles a different problem: the memory bottleneck. When AI agents work simultaneously across large codebases or hours of video, memory bandwidth becomes the chokepoint. Google addressed this by placing two TPU 8i chips on a single package. The result is double the compute power, double the memory, and double the memory bandwidth in the same rack format, which means significantly more performance per square meter of data center space. Ad Beyond hardware, Google is working to make TPUs easier to use. The company has released TorchTPU as open source , so PyTorch code should run on TPUs with minimal changes. Popular inference frameworks like vLLM and SGLang are also supported. Ad The expansion is a direct response to Google's strategic shift from treating TPUs as a purely internal tool to marketing them as a competitive platform for outside customers. The company now counts nearly 100 external TPU customers. A broader market trend is driving this push. As AI applications spread, the focus is shifting from expensive training runs to inference, meaning the day-to-day operation of models. Specialized chips like TPUs can play to their strengths in exactly this area. That's also why Amazon, Microsoft, and OpenAI are all developing their own accelerators. items.full: Most of the changes I make to my projects these days come in the form of PRs opened for me by Claude Code or Codex. The PR is my unit of work—I use them to bundle commits together, iterating on them until a feature is complete, document decisions and then merge the finished result. Today’s coding agents are great at writing PR descriptions. The problem is that they are too good. An agent-written PR description is accurate and comprehensive. It describes the problem, the detailed solution, and the steps taken to verify it. That’s a lot of information to absorb. It’s not necessarily slop, but it reads like slop! It’s very easy to spot an AI-written PR, and as with other forms of AI writing my instant reaction is best summarized as “I’m not reading all of that”. It doesn’t matter how accurate or useful the information is, I’m instantly put off by the thought that it will take me longer to read than it took the driving author to write... even when that driving author is me! I want human editorial judgement. I want someone to have thought just long enough about the PR to give me a human-approved introduction that helps me understand, at a high level, what the PR is for and whether it deserves more of my attention. I think I’ve found a low-effort way to do this that feels right. The HTML <details><summary> elements render as a collapsed heading (the summary) that can be expanded to view the larger piece of text. The code looks like this: < details > < summary > Claude Opus 5.5 </ summary > < h2 > The hook </ h2 > Plugins implement < code > register_agent_reference_types(datasette) </ code > ... </ details > When rendered, it looks like this : Crucially, <details><summary> is supported in GitHub Markdown . You can drop those tags directly into an issue comment or PR description and GitHub will hide the details and display just the summary plus an expansion arrow. I’ve started using this for my AI-generated pull requests. The opening paragraph of my PRs will be carefully selected to act as a high-level explanation of what’s going on—the shortest text a human can read that will help get them up to speed. I’ll sometimes throw in a screenshot as well, since images are often the best way to quickly illustrate a new feature. The full agent-written essay then follows in a <details><summary> . I use the model name and often the effort level as that summary, to make it abundantly clear what is going on—“Claude Opus 5.5 Medium” for example. My PRs don’t feel nearly as sloppy now! The information is all still there, but a reader can glance at it and get the top, human-curated information without their eyes glazing over at multiple paragraphs of agent-written details. I don’t always write the introduction myself—sometimes the agent has given me what I need already, hidden away in the avalanche of other text. My promise to the reader is that the short opener will represent my human judgement as to what is definitely worth their time. items.title: How to Build a Fast News Aggregation Site With Astro and WordPress
items.desc: Keep WordPress as a headless backend and let Astro render the front end to build a news aggregation site that loads fast and stays current. The post " How to Build a Fast News Aggregation Site With Astro and WordPress " first appeared on WP Mayor .
items.full: If you purchase through a link on our site, we may earn a commission . News aggregation sites ask a lot of whatever you build them on. They pull in hundreds or thousands of items from outside feeds, the content refreshes constantly, and visitors judge the result on two things: how fast it loads and how current it feels. WordPress is great at one half of that job. It fetches feeds, organizes content, deduplicates items, and runs imports on a schedule without breaking a sweat. Where it struggles is the front end, where a long and frequently-updating stream rendered through a full theme starts to feel slow. There is a clean way around this, and it has become a lot more practical in the last couple of years. Keep WordPress as your backend and hand the front end to Astro . You get the half of WordPress that does the real work, and a front end built from the ground up for speed. In this guide you will see how the two fit together, how to connect them, and how to solve the one problem that trips everyone up the first time, which is showing fresh content on a site that is mostly static. A news aggregator is one of the strongest candidates for a headless setup, and a better fit than a typical blog. It is worth being honest about when headless WordPress makes sense and when it is overkill, because the answer here lands firmly on the “yes” side. Start with the front end: it is read-only . Visitors don’t log in, comment, or fill out a form on the aggregated stream. The entire value of the site is fetching, organizing, and presenting other people’s content quickly, so serving it as fast static or cached HTML costs you nothing. WordPress is genuinely good at the fetching and organizing. There is a mature plugin ecosystem for pulling RSS and Atom feeds, deduplicating them, mapping fields, handling images, and scheduling the imports. That is real work you do not want to rebuild from scratch in a custom app. Astro, meanwhile, is built for exactly this kind of content-heavy, mostly-static site. It ships zero JavaScript by default , renders to fast static HTML, and lets you add interactivity only on the pages that need it. For a wall of feed items, that default is precisely what you want. On the WordPress side, the import engine is what matters. WP RSS Aggregator is the most established option, and the feature that makes it work cleanly in a headless build is Feed to Post . Feed to Post imports each feed item as a real WordPress post, or any custom post type you choose, with the content, featured image, taxonomies, and author filled in. Regular posts and custom post types are exposed through the WordPress REST API and through WPGraphQL automatically. So once your feeds are importing as posts, Astro can read them with no extra work on the WordPress side. The lightweight feed items that the free version stores are a different story. They are built for on-site display and are not exposed through the REST API by default. You can register them for REST yourself with a small filter, but importing as posts avoids the detour and gives you richer data to render. items.title: CSS Optimization: Is Using Declarations Just Once (UDJO) Still Effective Today?
items.desc: Is the technique inspired by the DRY principle by identifying and reducing (if not eliminating) CSS declaration repetition still a relevant optimization strategy? CSS Optimization: Is Using Declarations Just Once (UDJO) Still Effective Today? originally handwritten and published with love on CSS-Tricks . You should really get the newsletter as well.
items.full: NVIDIA L4 GPUs. 5-second cold starts. Scale to zero when idle. CSS optimization is a deceptive topic. On the one hand, it feels like something simple that we should already have all the tooling for — especially when it comes to minification. On the other hand, the idea that we already exploited “everything” there is around CSS optimization may be considered naive. Such a claim looks hard to defend for a language that evolves almost daily. In this article, I’d like to pick a technique that’s at least 18 years old — UDJO , or “using declarations just once.” Aware of an older source? Please comment! The technique is inspired by the principle of DRY , “don’t repeat yourself” , in that it works by identifying and reducing (if not eliminating) declaration repetition. So, if there’s something like display: flex and it appears two or more times, it gets reconciled in one rule: .example { display: flex; } .sample { display: flex; } …becomes: .example, .sample { display: flex; } The outcome of the technique depends on how intelligently the deduplication is done and how long the selectors are. Intelligence determines if UDJO leads to an actual maintainability advantage — can the change of a declaration really be done to all the selectors attached? And the selector length influences how big file size savings are. If you’re interested, my article on “DRY CSS” describes the mechanics in more detail. The question here is: Is UDJO still effective and still relevant today? Better Deduplicating Through Tooling When we try to answer this question, however, we end up with a problem: When sites are complex and their style sheet declarations have not been de-duplicated before, UDJO can require a lot of work. To save some time, I built tooling for this work. While it didn’t seem like it would immediately be as comprehensive as manually going through and testing style sheets, it seemed realistic enough that a tool could catch some repetition. Skipping ahead, I created CSS Dedup not only to identify repetition, but also to deduplicate what could safely be optimized (CSS Dedup has some documentation on this but in essence, deduplication affects selector locations, which is part of how the cascade works ). This, then, gives us some data: Is There Anything to Deduplicate in Modern CSS? For the first batch, I arbitrarily picked 20 websites to analyze. I then used CSS Dedup to check what the file size changes would be if we deduplicated what seemed provably safe, and also what seemed probably safe, but only if it led to file size savings. I picked those two options to provide the “natural” result of deduplication, but also the one site owners may be most interested in to reduce repetition but also decrease transfer size. After all, UDJO as a CSS optimization technique can improve both maintainability and performance. Important note: These values cannot be used to tell CSS quality —they depend on selector length and also on verifying if deduplication, in the respective case, actually leads to better maintainability. items.full: WordPress 7.2 Beta 5 is ready for download and testing! This beta release is intended for testing and development only. Please do not install, run, or test this version of WordPress on production or mission-critical websites. Instead, use a test environment or local site to explore the new features. You can test WordPress 7.2 Beta 5 in any of the following ways: The scheduled final release date for WordPress 7.2 is December 8, 2026 . The full release schedule can be found here . Your help testing Beta and RC versions is vital to making this release as stable and powerful as possible. Thank you to everyone who contributes by testing! For technical details on the issues addressed since Beta 4, see the following links: WordPress 7.2 Beta 5 continues refining the upcoming release with additional security, accessibility, and compatibility improvements. Recent changes include email notifications when application passwords are created, improved keyboard navigation in the WordPress admin toolbar, and accessibility refinements to Visual History. Additional fixes strengthen permissions for Notes reactions, improve compatibility with MP3 uploads, and address automatic update behavior in Git worktree installations. Learn more: Trac #63927 , Trac #66331 , Trac #65122 , Trac #66447 , Trac #46544 , Trac #66460 The new default theme, Ipsum, receives another round of improvements in WordPress 7.2 Beta 5. Accessibility enhancements include improved keyboard focus indicators and view transitions that respect reduced-motion preferences. Additional refinements to block styles and patterns provide greater design flexibility, while optimized stylesheets and other under-the-hood improvements help prepare the theme for its final release. Learn more: Trac #66631 , GitHub #198 , GitHub #187 , GitHub #180 WordPress 7.2 aims to fully support PHP 8.6, which is scheduled to be released on November 19, 2026. The WordPress project has a long history of being compatible with new versions of PHP as soon as possible, and this release is no different. As of the Beta 5 release, all known compatibility issues with PHP 8.6 have been resolved. While all of the known issues in WordPress have been addressed, you will need to verify that all of your plugins and themes are also compatible with PHP 8.6 prior to upgrading. Keep an eye on the Making WordPress Core blog in the coming days for more detailed information about what to look for. WordPress continues to encourage all users to run the latest and greatest versions of PHP. Testing for issues is a critical part of developing any software, and it’s a meaningful way for anyone to contribute – whether or not you have experience. Details on what to test in WordPress 7.2 are available here . If you encounter an issue, please share it in the Alpha/Beta area of the support forums. If you are comfortable submitting a reproducible bug report, you can do so via WordPress Trac . You can also check your issue against this list of known bugs . Curious about testing releases in general and how to get started? Follow along with the testing initiatives in Make Core and join the #core-test channel on Making WordPress Slack .
